title: Isolation assertions and burst safeguard protocol
content:
Context and problem statement:

We need a principled approach to let customers on Dedicated get predictable latency and bounded cost while still allowing controlled short-term bursts and fair isolation across tenants. Existing ideas (credit pools, soft reserve) have iterations in product, but we keep seeing two classes of failure in production tests: 

1) Silent degradation: a tenant quietly consumes spare capacity and pushes other tenants over their SLOs before throttles kick in.
2) Surge collapse: simultaneous microbursts across tenants exhaust warm pools and cause long tail latency spikes during prewarm recovery.

Goal of this doc:
- Propose a combined design ("Isolation Assertions + Burst Safeguard Protocol") that:
  - Lets tenants safely borrow short-term capacity without violating higher-priority tenants' latency SLOs;
  - Provides clear, observable invariants (assertions) for isolation so SRE/CS can reason about regressions;
  - Fits into Dedicated's existing lease/reservation model and can be rolled out incrementally.

Design summary (high level):
- Isolation Assertions: lightweight, runtime-checked constraints attached to tenant routes. Each assertion expresses a measurable invariant (e.g., p99 <= 80ms for model X on lane Y, or max concurrent tokens = N). Assertions are enforced by the scheduler and emitted as metrics (assertion_violations).

- Burst Safeguard Protocol (BSP): a coordinated short-lived credit+quota mechanism with three components:
  1) Local burst tokens: per-tenant short-term token buckets representing immediate burst allowance (sourced from ephemeral warm pool).
  2) Asserted headroom reservation: when a tenant requests tokens beyond local allowance, scheduler consults isolation assertions and, if safe, temporarily assigns a guarded slot from a shared ephemeral reservoir. This assignment is tagged with a reclaim deadline and a soft-fallback route.
  3) Circuit manager: monitors assertion metrics and revokes/soft-degrades burst assignments if any dependent assertion starts trending toward violation. Revocation is prioritized by SLA tier and assertion severity.

Why this is different:
- We focus on observable invariants (assertions) rather than opaque budgets. That makes post-incident debugging much easier and ties safety to SLOs instead of arbitrary quotas.
- The BSP gives a short, bounded lending model (tokens + deadline) that avoids long-lived overcommitment.

User stories / acceptance criteria:
- As an SRE, I can see assertion_violations in Console for any tenant and map them to burst assignments in the same time window.
- As a customer, I can opt-in to allow my routes to consume ephemeral burst tokens up to X for Y minutes with clear billing visibility.
- As a platform engineer, I can revoke all ephemeral assignments for lower-tier tenants within 5s of a high-priority assertion violation.

Non-goals:
- This doc does not propose a new long-term reservation market or change contractual Reserved Capacity semantics.
- We are not replacing existing backfills or preemption policies; BSP augments them.

Detailed behavior and APIs:
- Assertion model:
  - Assertion definition fields: route_id, metric (latency/concurrency/token-rate), threshold, evaluation_window, severity, linked_slo_id.
  - Assertions are submitted via Console or API (PATCH /tenant/{id}/assertions).
  - Runtime: scheduler evaluates assertions using sliding windows from telemetry. Violations become first-class events.

- Burst tokens lifecycle:
  - Local tokens: refill rate tied to tenant commit tier + historical usage; stored in local scheduler instance.
  - Ephemeral reservoir: a global pool per-pool (not per-tenant) with configurable size and preemption policy.
  - Assignment: ephemeral allocation requests include desired duration and a fallback policy (route to cheaper model, queue, or deny). If accepted, BSP issues a signed token with expiry metadata that is checked by serving nodes.

- Circuit manager rules (examples):
  - If any lane's p95 latency exceeds asserted threshold by 20% for >30s, immediately reclaim ephemeral assignments from tenants with severity <= medium, and place them on soft-degrade route.
  - If multiple high-severity assertions start trending, enter a global conservation mode that reduces ephemeral reservoir capacity by 50% and raises token prices (billing visible to customers).

Observability and telemetry:
- New metrics: assertion_count, assertion_violations, ephemeral_allocations_total, ephemeral_reclaims_total, allocation_latency_seconds.
- Dashboards: per-tenant assertion timeline (overlaid with burst token assignments), pool health view (reservoir fill, churn), and a global incident panel keyed by assertion severity.
- Tracing: allocation events should carry tenant_id/assertion_id so traces map to specific decisions.

Billing and product/UX implications:
- Ephemeral allocations billed at a visible premium; Console shows a predicted cost before assignment.
- Customers can set guardrails (max_burst_cost_per_day) and automatic opt-out triggers (if cost > threshold).

Operational runbook sketch (for SRE/ops):
1) Detection: assertion_violations fire -> automated playbook suggests reclaim options and lists currently allocated ephemeral tokens.
2) Immediate action: toggle GUI button to drain ephemeral reservoir for a pool or revoke by tenant tier.
3) Postmortem: map violations to allocation timeline and decisions; include billing changes if cost incentives caused aggressive bursts.

Rollout plan (phased):
- Phase 0 (canary): expose assertion telemetry only (no enforcement) for 6 pools; collect baseline metrics and false positive rate.
- Phase 1 (beta): local tokens + visibility, allow customers to opt-in to BSP in 2 regions; enforcement limited to soft-fallbacks.
- Phase 2 (general availability): full BSP enforcement, circuit manager active, Console controls for opt-in/limits and billing.

Risks and mitigations:
- Risk: false assertion violations cause unnecessary revocations -> mitigation: conservative thresholds in canary and human-in-the-loop overrides.
- Risk: customers misunderstand pricing -> mitigation: UI previews, emails before first charge, and default safe caps.
- Risk: complexity in scheduler -> mitigation: keep BSP allocator as a thin layer that calls existing lease manager; limit statefulness (use signed tokens).

Open questions:
- What granularity of assertion is useful? per-route? per-model? per-tenant? (proposal: default per-route, allow aggregate tenant assertions)
- Should ephemeral reservoir be per-region only or per-pool+region? (proposal: start per-pool+region)
- How to compute safe ephemeral reservoir size? (proposal: telemetry-driven: base on 99th percentile spare capacity over trailing 7 days)

Next steps / action items:
- Product: finalize assertion schema and Console UI mockups (owner: Evelyn) — due 2025-11-18.
- Eng (scheduler): prototype signed ephemeral token format and enforcement hooks (owner: Marco) — spike by 2025-11-29.
- SRE: draft runbook pages and dashboard templates (owner: Samir) — draft by 2025-12-05.

Notes / stray thoughts (working):
- Consider allowing customers to attach "burst policies" that map assertions to preferred fallback routes (e.g., route to quantized variant first).
- We may be able to use existing lease revocation signals for fast reclaim; signed tokens help avoid cross-process state locking.

References and related work:
- Internal: dedicated/ephemeral-warm-pool-notes (confluence)
- Related PRs: github.com/redwood-inference/dedicated-scheduler/pull/197 (prewarm heuristics), PR#213 (token signing)
- Long-term: possible integration with reserved-capacity marketplace (not in scope)

If this direction looks promising I can convert assertions into a small OpenAPI schema and a Console mock to iterate with CS before a scheduler spike.
